title: DeepMind's AI Agent Hunts Drug-Resistant Bacteria and Surfaces a New Candidate
excerpt: Using its Antigravity platform and the ProtNLM model, DeepMind biologists filtered millions of uncharacterized proteins to a single antimicrobial peptide lead — now in lab validation, with no results yet.
body:
• Google DeepMind biologists used its Antigravity agentic platform to identify a candidate antimicrobial peptide in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae; the lead is now undergoing wet-lab validation.
  • The agent filtered millions of uncharacterized proteins in the UniProt database using DeepMind's ProtNLM model and settled on a 97-amino-acid bacteriocin, UniProt ID A0A0U0D591, from the Lactococcin 972 family.
  • Antimicrobial resistance could result in an estimated 10 million deaths a year globally by 2050, according to the estimate DeepMind cites — the problem the search is aimed at.
  • The candidate is a computational prediction, not a medicine: DeepMind says it is a biologically plausible lead that still requires lab validation, and it has given no results or timeline.

Google DeepMind is using AI agents to hunt for new weapons against drug-resistant bacteria. In a technical walkthrough published on October 15, the company showed how its biologists used Google Antigravity, its agentic development platform, to work through millions of uncharacterized proteins and surface a candidate antimicrobial peptide — a possible starting point for a new class of antibiotic.

The stakes are the reason the work matters. Antimicrobial resistance — bacteria, viruses and fungi evolving to outsmart the drugs used against them — could result in an estimated 10 million deaths a year globally by 2050, according to the estimate DeepMind cites. A Forbes analysis published October 31 makes the same point from the clinic's side: if new drug innovation does not keep pace with microbial evolution, the result is drug-resistant infections that even the strongest existing treatments cannot clear. Antimicrobial peptides, particularly bacteriocins, are a promising alternative because they attack fundamental vulnerabilities in competing bacteria — cell envelopes and essential internal machinery — that pathogens find harder to evolve resistance against.

How the agent ran the search

The session began with a focused goal set by the researcher: find and computationally validate novel antimicrobial peptides in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae. The human steered the strategy, deciding which questions to ask; the agent handled the cross-database work. Using ProtNLM, a DeepMind model that predicts a protein's function directly from its amino-acid sequence, the agent scanned the UniProt database, which holds millions of sequences whose function has never been characterized, and filtered them down to a shortlist.

The candidate it landed on is a bacteriocin with UniProt ID A0A0U0D591, a peptide 97 amino acids long from the Lactococcin 972 family, with predicted activity against pathogens involved in respiratory tract infections. The agent then checked the candidate for novelty using the BLAST comparison service, which confirmed it did not meaningfully resemble any manually reviewed protein. It pulled the candidate's predicted 3D structure from the AlphaFold database and found its fold closely matches an experimentally determined bacteriocin. It also examined the genes flanking the candidate and found them arranged as part of a working bacteriocin system — the kind of contextual evidence biologists look for before spending lab time. From the literature, the agent proposed the peptide may act by targeting bacterial cell division, and it drafted the bench protocol for testing: protein expression, susceptibility testing, target engagement and toxicity assays.

The tool behind it

Antigravity is DeepMind's attempt to compress a fragmented workflow — custom scripts, exported files, separate structure-viewing software — into a single session. The walkthrough also introduced a Biomolecular Structure Viewer embedded in the platform, a shared 3D canvas where researcher and agent can highlight regions of a protein together. According to the Antigravity science page, the platform connects to more than 30 life-science databases, and Google is giving 10,000 scientists free access to its frontier model in Antigravity at its highest usage tier.

What this does not yet prove

DeepMind is careful about the limits, and readers should be too. The company characterizes the candidate as "a biologically plausible lead backed by structural and genomic evidence" that "still requires wet lab validation." The walkthrough is a demonstration chosen by Google to present its platform; the candidate exists only as predictions at this stage, and DeepMind has published no experimental results and no timeline for the lab tests. The candidate from the walkthrough, along with others found through the same process, is now in wet-lab validation, where DeepMind says experimental results will provide the ultimate test of the agent's analysis.

The broader significance is the workflow, not any single molecule: a search that used to take days of scripting and file-shuffling across disconnected tools happened in one supervised session. Whether that speed produces actual drugs depends on results that have not yet arrived.
